source_read: PDF of the PubMed Central author manuscript (22 pages; cited as AM p. N = PDF page): all text read in a pdftotext extraction; every number used checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi, including Fig. 1 (insert card, AM p. 15, also at 300 dpi), Fig. 2 (AM p. 16) and the landscape Tables 1-3 (AM pp. 17-22). For the two claims that also cite Morrison (2025) and the other drug-checking studies, only the Park parts were checked.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of Park et al.; two attributions to the review need softening. (1) 'not one month, as the review says': Park's own abstract says participants completed a survey after one month, and its hypothesis, Methods and Table 2 title speak of a one-month follow-up (AM pp. 1, 3, 4, 19); the mean of 56 days (22.1% within one month) is only in the Results (AM p. 6). The review repeats the paper's framing. (2) 'the review's 96% is the figure for all 103 at the start': Park's own abstract gives solitary use '96% vs. 68%' (AM p. 1); 96% matches either all 103 at baseline (99, 96.1%) or the 68 completers (95.6%, Table 1), while the paired figure for the 59 who used opioids at follow-up is 94.9% (Table 3). Better: 'the review repeats the abstract's 96%, a baseline from a larger denominator; paired, 94.9% to 67.8%'. Scope: the six-month against one-month window applies to the drug-use items (benzodiazepines, opioids, injection); using alone and overdose were asked about the past month at both visits (AM p. 5, 2.2.4).
claims.note: Park part only (the Morrison review parts are not this source). All Park numbers check on the rendered tables: 68 of 103 followed up (66.0%); solitary use 56/59 (94.9%) to 40/59 (67.8%), p < 0.001; benzodiazepine use 15/68 (22.1%) to 5/68 (7.4%), p < 0.01 (abstract p = 0.008); women who used no strip, at-least-daily illicit opioid use 9/11 (81.8%) to 4/11 (36.4%), not significant; non-fatal overdose 6/68 (8.8%) to 1/68 (1.5%), not significant; harm-reduction behaviour after a positive result 33/48 (68.8%). The baseline benzodiazepine figure in Table 3 (22.1%) equals the past-six-month figure among completers in Table 1 (22.1%), which confirms the Methods' six-month baseline window even though Table 3's footnote marks every row 'past month'. The insert card (Fig. 1) lists mixing drugs (alcohol, benzodiazepines) as an overdose risk and not using alone and having people check on you among its tips, and the micro-counselling addressed using alone and mixing alcohol with opioids (AM p. 4), as the claim says.

anchors.locator: 2. Methods, 1st paragraph; 2.1 FIT study recruitment and data collection, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Pilot nested in a cohort of street-based cis-gender women who sold or traded sex in the past 6 months, recruited by targeted sampling from a mobile van in Baltimore, April 2018 to February 2019; FIT eligibility: illicit opioid use in the past month. Primary prespecified outcome: number of non-fatal overdoses.

After the baseline survey: 5-10 minutes of strip training plus harm-reduction micro-counselling tailored to reported behaviour (e.g. mixing alcohol with opioids, using alone), with emphasis on test doses, having someone nearby with naloxone and polysubstance use; an insert card (Fig. 1) listing mixing drugs (alcohol, benzodiazepines) as an overdose risk and not using alone among safety tips; 5 strips, injection equipment and two doses of naloxone.

anchors.locator: 2.2.2 Substance use; 2.2.4 Risk behaviors and overdose
anchors.extracted: Drug use (including benzodiazepine pills) asked for the past 6 months at pretest and the past month at posttest; solitary use, asking someone to check, and overdose 'to the point of passing out' asked for the past month at both visits; overdose coded as at least one.
Follow-up completed on average 56 days after baseline, 22.1% within the one-month goal; 68 of 103 completed (Table 1). Younger women and those injecting opioid pills were more often lost.

anchors.locator: Table 3, Total (n = 68) and 'Did not use any FTS (n = 11)' columns
anchors.extracted: Total: solitary use 56 (94.9%) to 40 (67.8%), p < 0.001, among the 59 who used opioids at follow-up; benzodiazepine use 15 (22.1%) to 5 (7.4%), p < 0.01; non-fatal overdose 6 (8.8%) to 1 (1.5%), not significant. No strip used (n = 11): at-least-daily illicit opioid use 9 (81.8%) to 4 (36.4%), not significant.

anchors.locator: Table 1, rows 'Snort/swallowed benzodiazepine pills' (past 6 months block) and, AM p. 18, 'Solitary drug use'
anchors.extracted: Benzodiazepine pills in the past 6 months: 22 of 103 (21.4%), 22.1% of the 68 completers, the same as Table 3's baseline; solitary use 99 of 103 (96.1%), 95.6% of completers.
Abstract: survey 'after one month'; solitary drug use '96% vs. 68%'; benzodiazepine use 22% to 7% (p = 0.008); overdose change not mentioned.
Pretest-posttest design with a single follow-up and no control group; low participation and sub-optimal retention; possible social desirability and recall bias.

claims.overstatement: None for the Park part. The claim's wording ('named at least one safer action', 'used the tested drugs') follows Table 2. Two cautions the claim could carry: the categories overlap (33 safer action and 30 used the tested drugs among 48, select all that apply, about any of up to five positive results), so the text's gloss that the 30 used 'without behavioral modifications' (AM p. 7) cannot hold for all of them; and the question is described as select-all-that-apply in the Methods and Table 2 (AM pp. 5, 19) but as open-ended in the Results (AM p. 7).
claims.note: Recomputed: 33/48 = 68.8%, 30/48 = 62.5%, 15/48 = 31.3%, 10/48 = 20.8%, 5/48 = 10.4%, 3/48 = 6.3%, 6/48 = 12.5%, 2/48 = 4.2%; 21/24 = 87.5%. 'Did not use drugs' after a positive result 6 (printed 12.6%, 6/48 = 12.5%) = 3 threw out + 3 sold. Withdrawal was the most common reason for using as intended (12 of the 30, 40.0%); the further reasons are given over a denominator of 12 (5/12 enjoyed fentanyl, 2/12 'fentanyl habit', 4/12 doubted the result), which looks like a slip for 30. Negative results: 29 women had at least one (Table 2), 24 answered (5 missing), and the text says 'of the 25 women' while giving 87.5% (21/24).

anchors.extracted: Five strips with training, tailored micro-counselling and two doses of naloxone; follow-up on average 56 days later; recruitment April 2018 to February 2019.

48 women with at least one positive result answered: 30 (62.5%) used the drugs as intended, 12 of them (40.0%) to relieve withdrawal; 15 (31.3%) used a smaller amount, 10 (20.8%) went slower, 5 (10.4%) did a tester shot, 3 (6.3%) asked someone to check on them, 6 (12.5%) told others, 3 (6.3%) threw the drugs out, 3 (6.3%) sold them, 2 (4.2%) stopped going to that dealer.

anchors.locator: Table 2, positive-result and negative-result blocks with footnotes (AM p. 20)
anchors.extracted: After a positive result (n = 48, select all that apply): harm-reduction behaviour 33 (68.8%), used the tested drugs 30 (62.5%), did not use 6 (12.6%), cessation (stopped using or entered treatment) 0. After a negative result (n = 24, 5 missing of 29): used the tested drugs 21 (87.5%), harm-reduction behaviour 2 (8.4%), did not use 2 (8.3%).

Women with at least one positive or negative result were asked what they did after the result, select all that apply (harm-reduction behaviours, giving away or selling, continuing to use the tested drugs); self-report at follow-up, results not checked.
Of the women with at least one negative result ('of the 25'), 21 (87.5%) used their drugs as intended; 1 of 24 used a smaller amount and 1 went slower.

claims.overstatement: One label is wrong: '(4 to 1, by the editors' subtraction)' - Table 3 prints these counts in its 'Used at least 1 FTS (n = 57)' column (4 (7.0%) to 1 (1.8%)), so they are the paper's figures, not an editors' calculation (same in the magnitude). Otherwise the Park part is worded carefully: no comparison group, counselling on overdose risk, not significant, absent from the abstract.
claims.note: Recomputed: 68/103 = 66.0%; 6/68 = 8.8%, 1/68 = 1.5%; 4/57 = 7.0%, 1/57 = 1.8%; 2/11 = 18.2%. The prespecified primary outcome was the number of non-fatal overdoses (AM p. 4), but it was analysed as any overdose in the past month (AM p. 5), and no test statistic or p-value is given for it; the overdose row's percentages use 68 although the table section's footnote says 'among n = 59 who reported opioid use at follow-up' (solitary use and asking someone to check use 59). The Discussion describes the change as 'six times lower', not significant (AM p. 8); the abstract does not report it. Baseline overdose among all 103 was 10 (9.7%) (Table 1).

anchors.extracted: The primary prespecified outcome was the number of non-fatal overdoses.
At both visits, overdoses in the past month 'to the point of passing out', coded as any (at least one).

anchors.locator: Table 3, row 'Non-fatal overdose', all three column pairs
anchors.extracted: Total (n = 68): 6 (8.8%) to 1 (1.5%), no significance mark; used at least one strip (n = 57): 4 (7.0%) to 1 (1.8%); used none (n = 11): 2 (18.2%) to 0 (0.0%). No comparison between the strata.

anchors.locator: 3.1 Pretest-posttest differences, continued (1st lines); 4. Discussion, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Changes in non-fatal overdose were in the expected direction but not significant; the Discussion calls overdose six times lower at follow-up, attributing non-significance to short follow-up and small sample.

The abstract reports significant reductions in daily opioid use, injection frequency, benzodiazepine use and solitary use, but not the overdose result, and concludes that strip-based interventions hold potential in reducing overdose risk.
Pretest-posttest design, single follow-up, no control group; suboptimal retention and small sample may leave the analysis underpowered.

reporting_issues.note: Table 1 completers: benzodiazepine pills (past-6-months block) 22.1%, IDU past 6 months 50.0% (AM p. 17) = Table 3 baselines 15 (22.1) and 34 (50.0) (AM p. 21), whose footnote reads 'past month'. Solitary use and overdose were past month at both visits (AM p. 5), so the window problem does not touch them.
Addition: the abstract's 96% also matches the baseline of the 68 completers (95.6%, Table 1, AM p. 18), not only all 103 (96.1%); either way it is not paired with the 67.8% of 59.
Text AM p. 7 '22.8% to 7.40%'; Table 3 users 13 (22.8) to 4 (7.0), total 15 (22.1) to 5 (7.4). AM p. 8 refers the non-significant changes to Table 2.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I critical overall (confounding critical: single arm, co-delivered counselling and card on the same behaviours, non-users changed as much). Domain judgments agree. Wilson intervals in the analysis field reproduce (57/68 73.3-90.7; 33/48 54.7-80.1; 30/48 48.4-74.8; 65/68 87.8-98.5).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: 'short-term effectiveness' (AM p. 8) and the abstract's conclusion rest on an uncontrolled pre-post comparison with mismatched recall windows; the primary outcome is absent from the abstract; the Discussion calls the non-significant overdose change 'six times lower'.

missed: The Results text calls the after-result question 'an open-ended survey question' (AM p. 7, 5th and 6th paragraphs), while the Methods and Table 2 describe a select-all-that-apply question (AM pp. 5, 19); the format affects how the 69% and 63% should be read.

Table 3's overdose row uses 68 as its denominator (6/68 = 8.8%, 1/68 = 1.5%) although the section footnote says 'among n = 59 who reported opioid use at follow-up', which fits the solitary-use and asking-someone rows; no McNemar statistic or p-value is given for overdose (AM pp. 21-22).

The follow-up is called one month throughout (abstract, AM p. 1; hypothesis, AM p. 3; Methods, AM p. 4; Table 2 title, AM p. 19; Fig. 2, AM p. 16) although the mean was 56 days; Table 2's 'Used FTS in past month' therefore may not cover the whole interval. Claims citing 'not one month, as the review says' should note that the paper itself says one month.

Table 3's needle-exchange row does not add up: total 29 (42.7%) to 22 (32.4%), but strata 17 (77.3%) + 2 (66.7%) = 19 at baseline and 13 + 1 = 14 at follow-up, percentages that fit denominators of 22 and 3 (AM p. 22). Alcohol frequency is labelled 'at least daily' in Table 3 but was dichotomized as at least weekly in the Methods (AM pp. 5, 21). Not relevant to the current claims.
